blocks.content: Before a single EC2 instance, a single S3 bucket, or a single line of Terraform, there is one question worth answering properly: what is cloud computing actually, beyond the marketing phrase. This entire course is built on top of the answer.
1. Cloud Computing, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: 1. Cloud Computing, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: Cloud computing is the on demand delivery of computing resources, servers, storage, databases, networking, and software, over the internet, with a provider owning and operating the underlying physical infrastructure on your behalf.

Instead of purchasing physical servers, racking them in a data center, and maintaining them yourself, you request exactly the computing capacity you need from a provider such as AWS, and that capacity becomes available within minutes.

This is a genuinely fundamental shift from how computing infrastructure worked for decades before cloud computing existed, where any new capacity required a real, physical procurement process measured in weeks or months, not minutes.

Every service covered across the remaining eighteen modules of this course, from EC2 to S3 to Lambda, is ultimately an expression of this one core idea: computing resources delivered on demand, over the internet, without you owning the physical hardware.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784735996347-614500138.png
blocks.alt: Cloud computing given its own full depth

blocks.content: 2. Before and After: What Actually Changed
blocks.text: 2. Before and After: What Actually Changed

blocks.content: Before cloud computing, running an application meant owning or leasing physical servers, housing them in a data center you controlled, and hiring staff to rack, cable, cool, power, and maintain that hardware for its entire operational life.

Capacity planning was a genuinely high stakes guessing game: buy too little hardware and the application falls over under real load, buy too much and expensive, depreciating equipment sits idle, both outcomes representing real, wasted money.

Cloud computing replaces that owned, fixed hardware with rented, elastic capacity. The provider owns the physical reality, the servers, the data centers, the networking, and you consume exactly the capacity you need, precisely when you need it.

This shift, from owning fixed infrastructure to renting elastic capacity, is the single most important mental model to carry into every subsequent module of this course, since nearly every AWS service is a specific expression of this same underlying shift.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784735999656-546448915.png
blocks.alt: A data center you own versus a provider you rent exact capacity from

blocks.content: 3. A Real Cloud Computing Example

Consider a team that needs a new server to run a web application. Under the old, pre cloud model, this requires submitting a purchase request, waiting for hardware to arrive, physically installing it, and configuring an operating system, a process easily taking weeks.

Under cloud computing, that same team logs into the AWS console, or runs a single command through the AWS CLI, and has a fully running server available within minutes, with no physical hardware ever touched by anyone on the team.

If that server turns out to be undersized for real traffic, resizing it is another few minutes of work, not another multi week procurement cycle. If it is no longer needed at all, it can be terminated instantly, and billing for it stops immediately.

This compression of a multi week process into minutes, repeatable indefinitely and reversible just as quickly, is the single most immediately tangible benefit cloud computing delivers, and it is the foundation every other benefit covered in this module builds on.

# The old way: weeks of procurement, racking, and configuration
# The cloud way: a server running in minutes
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 --instance-type t2.micro --count 1

blocks.content: 4. The Five Defining Characteristics

The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology defines cloud computing through five essential characteristics, a definition worth knowing since it captures precisely what separates genuine cloud computing from merely renting a server somewhere.

On demand self service means a user can provision computing capabilities automatically, without requiring human interaction with the provider, exactly as demonstrated in the previous section's single command example.

Broad network access means capabilities are available over the network through standard mechanisms, pooling means the provider's resources serve multiple customers using a multi tenant model, elasticity means capacity can scale rapidly in both directions, and measured service means usage is tracked and billed precisely.

A hosting arrangement missing any one of these five characteristics, for example one requiring a phone call and a multi day wait for new capacity, would not genuinely qualify as cloud computing under this definition, regardless of how it is marketed.

5. Public, Private, and the Rest of This Module
blocks.text: 5. Public, Private, and the Rest of This Module

blocks.content: Cloud computing as defined in this topic describes the general model, but it can actually be implemented in several different ways, distinguished by who owns the underlying infrastructure and who else shares access to it.

The next few topics in this module build directly on this foundation: Why Cloud covers the practical business case for adopting this model, and Cloud Deployment Models covers the specific ways this model can actually be implemented in practice.
Every one of those topics assumes the definition established here, on demand, self service, elastic, measured computing resources delivered over a network, as their shared, common starting point.

Keeping this definition precise, rather than the looser, marketing driven cloud language often used casually, is what makes every subsequent, more advanced topic in this course build on solid ground rather than a vague impression.
6. A Common Mistake: Just Someone Else's Computer
blocks.text: 6. A Common Mistake: Just Someone Else's Computer

blocks.content: A common, dismissive oversimplification is describing the cloud as simply someone else's computer, a phrase that captures a grain of truth but misses nearly everything that actually makes cloud computing valuable and different from traditional hosting.

Traditional hosting, such as renting a single dedicated server from a hosting company, genuinely is just someone else's computer: fixed capacity, manual provisioning, and no meaningful elasticity, pooling, or measured, granular billing.

Cloud computing, defined by the five characteristics covered earlier in this topic, is a fundamentally different arrangement: elastic, self service, and billed by precise, granular usage, none of which describe a single rented dedicated server.

Understanding this distinction precisely matters because the five characteristics are exactly what unlocks the practical benefits, covered in the very next topic, that make cloud computing genuinely transformative for how organizations build and run software.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736004824-740184619.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of thinking of the cloud as just someone else's computer

blocks.content: 7. Where AWS Fits Into This Definition
blocks.text: 7. Where AWS Fits Into This Definition

blocks.content: Amazon Web Services, the subject of this entire course, is one specific, extremely widely adopted implementation of the cloud computing model just defined, alongside other major providers such as Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform.

AWS satisfies every one of the five characteristics covered earlier: self service through the console, CLI, and API, broad network access globally, massive resource pooling across millions of customers, rapid elasticity, and precisely measured, usage based billing.

This course focuses specifically on AWS, not because the underlying cloud computing concepts differ meaningfully between providers, but because AWS's specific services, terminology, and implementation details are what a real, hands on engineer needs to master.

Every concept introduced generically in this module, on demand provisioning, elasticity, measured billing, will be revisited throughout this course in its specific AWS form, such as EC2 for provisioning and CloudWatch for measurement.
8. The Historical Shift That Made This Possible
blocks.text: 8. The Historical Shift That Made This Possible

blocks.content: Cloud computing as defined in this topic did not emerge overnight. It became practical only once virtualization technology matured enough to let a single physical server safely and efficiently run many isolated, independent virtual machines simultaneously.

This virtualization layer is precisely what enables the resource pooling characteristic covered earlier in this topic: many customers' workloads sharing the same physical hardware while remaining completely isolated from each other's data and processes.

AWS launched its first services in the mid 2000s, and the model has matured enormously since, expanding from raw compute and storage into the vast catalog of managed services covered across the remaining eighteen modules of this course.

Understanding this history briefly is useful context: cloud computing is not a recent trend but a now mature, well proven model with roughly two decades of continuous, real world production use behind it.
9. Cloud Computing and the Software Development Lifecycle
blocks.text: 9. Cloud Computing and the Software Development Lifecycle

blocks.content: Cloud computing changes not just where infrastructure lives, but how software itself gets built, tested, and shipped, since developers can now provision realistic, production like environments on demand for testing rather than sharing a small number of scarce, fixed environments.

A development team can spin up an entire, isolated test environment for a single pull request, run automated tests against it, and tear it down immediately afterward, a workflow genuinely impractical under a traditional, fixed hardware model.

This capability directly enables the CI CD practices covered in dedicated depth in Module 11 later in this course, where automated pipelines routinely create and destroy real infrastructure as a normal, everyday part of shipping software.

Recognizing this connection between cloud computing's on demand nature and modern software development practices sets useful context for why this course later dedicates entire modules to CI CD and Infrastructure as Code.
10. A Second Real Example: Disaster Recovery
blocks.text: 10. A Second Real Example: Disaster Recovery

blocks.content: Consider a company that, under a traditional owned infrastructure model, would need a second, largely idle data center purely as insurance against the first one failing, a genuinely expensive proposition given how rarely such a failure actually occurs.

Under cloud computing, that same company can maintain a minimal, low cost standby environment that only scales up to full capacity if the primary environment genuinely fails, paying only a small ongoing cost for readiness rather than the full cost of a duplicate, idle data center.

This pattern, covered in complete depth in Module 13, High Availability and Disaster Recovery, would be prohibitively expensive to replicate under a traditional, owned infrastructure model, precisely because idle owned hardware still costs its full price regardless of use.

This is a second, genuinely concrete illustration, alongside the server provisioning example earlier in this topic, of exactly how the on demand, measured nature of cloud computing changes what is practically and economically achievable.
11. Common Terminology Worth Knowing Early

Provisioning refers to the act of creating and configuring a new resource, exactly the process demonstrated in this topic's real example, and it is a term used constantly throughout the rest of this course.

Elastic, already introduced as one of the five defining characteristics, describes a resource's ability to scale its capacity up or down automatically or on demand, a term applied throughout later modules to describe specific AWS services with this capability.

Managed service describes an AWS offering where AWS itself handles a meaningful portion of the underlying operational burden, directly connecting to the IaaS, PaaS, SaaS spectrum covered in a later topic in this module.

Introducing this vocabulary now, even briefly, means later modules can use these terms directly without needing to redefine them each time, keeping the course's pace efficient once this foundational module is complete.

12. Cloud Computing Beyond Just Servers

While the earlier example focused on a single server, cloud computing extends to nearly every category of computing resource: storage, covered in Module 4, databases, covered in Module 5, and networking, covered in Module 6, are all delivered under this exact same on demand model.

This breadth is genuinely important to internalize early. Cloud computing is not simply a new way to rent servers. It is a new way to consume the entire computing stack, from raw compute up through fully managed, higher level services.

Later modules in this course, particularly Serverless Architecture in Module 12, take this on demand model to its logical extreme, where you no longer manage servers at all, only the code that runs in response to events.

Recognizing this full breadth now, rather than mentally narrowing cloud computing to just servers, sets the right expectation for the genuinely wide scope of services this nineteen module course goes on to cover in full depth.
13. Why This Definition Matters for Real Engineering Decisions
blocks.text: 13. Why This Definition Matters for Real Engineering Decisions

blocks.content: Understanding cloud computing precisely, rather than loosely, directly affects real engineering decisions made throughout a career working with AWS, particularly around cost, scaling, and architectural tradeoffs covered later in this course.

An engineer who understands elasticity as a defining characteristic, not just a nice bonus feature, designs applications that genuinely take advantage of scaling capacity up and down, rather than provisioning a single fixed size server and never revisiting that decision.

An engineer who understands measured service precisely understands why AWS billing can fluctuate meaningfully month to month, and builds the monitoring habits, covered in Module 8, needed to track and control that fluctuation deliberately.

This precise, foundational understanding, established in this very first topic, is what every subsequent module in this course assumes and builds directly on top of, rather than needing to be relearned or clarified later.
14. The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Cloud computing is a precise, defined model, on demand, self service, elastic, measured computing resources delivered over a network, not merely a vague marketing phrase for someone else's computer somewhere.

Every AWS service covered across the remaining eighteen modules of this course is a specific implementation of this one underlying model, and returning to this definition whenever a new service feels unfamiliar is a genuinely useful grounding habit.

The next topic, Why Cloud, builds directly on this definition, making the concrete, practical business case for why organizations actually choose to adopt this model over traditional, owned infrastructure.
Keep the minutes instead of weeks image from this topic's real example firmly in mind. It is the single most tangible, memorable illustration of exactly what cloud computing changes in practice.

On demand, self service, elastic, measured: the five words this entire course is built on.
Cloud computing is a precise model, not a marketing phrase.

blocks.title: What Is Cloud Computing, In Full
points: Cloud computing is the on demand delivery of computing resources over the internet, with a provider owning the underlying physical infrastructure.
It is precisely defined by five characteristics: on demand self service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service.
It represents a fundamental shift from owning fixed infrastructure to renting elastic capacity, compressing weeks long procurement into minutes.
Describing the cloud as just someone else's computer misses what actually makes it valuable: elasticity, self service, and precise, granular billing.
AWS is one major implementation of this model, and this entire course covers its specific services in full depth, starting with the practical case for adopting cloud computing in the very next topic.
